transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, Doc, I... I appreciate you seeing me, honestly, because I didn't really know where else to go at this point. I'm here because... well, it sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but I just cannot stop seeing this... this rough, sunken-looking patch right here on my face. 

I mean, I work construction, right? Have for thirty years, so I know I'm gonna have some wear and tear from the sun and the dust, but this is different. Every single time I walk past a mirror, or look in the rearview of my truck, or—God forbid—someone takes a photo of me at a family barbecue or something, it is literally all I can focus on. It just looks like this whole side of my face is completely old and beat-up, like it's just caving in and ruined. 

And I spend so much time just staring at it in the bathroom, you know, turning my head this way and that way under the vanity light, trying to figure out how bad it is and if I can hide it. But the part that really drives me up the wall, the reason I'm sitting in this chair right now, is that my wife, the guys on the crew, my kids... they all look at me like I've got two heads when I bring it up. They keep saying they barely notice anything at all, or they tell me it's just a shadow, or normal aging. But I know what I'm looking at, you know? I'm not blind. I can see it clear as day in every single picture, and I just can't stop thinking about how terrible it looks, no matter how many times people tell me I'm making a big deal out of nothing. It's just constantly on my mind.
How much does this concern about the appearance of that patch on your face interfere with your day-to-day life or cause you emotional distress?

Well, it's... it's messing with a lot of things, honestly. More than I want to admit to my wife, anyway. Like, take my mornings, right? I've got to be on the site early, usually by 6 AM, which means I'm up at 4:30. But lately, instead of just grabbing my coffee and my boots, I’m standing there in the bathroom, just staring at this patch, trying to see if the lighting makes it look worse today. I'll turn my head, maybe try to rub some lotion on it or something to see if it smooths out... and before I know it, twenty, thirty minutes have gone by. I’ve actually been late getting out the door for my construction jobs because of it, which is bad, you know? You can't be late on a crew. The foreman starts barking, and I can't exactly tell him I was staring in the mirror. 

And then when I'm actually at work, if someone pulls out a phone for a site photo—like when we finish a big pour or top out a frame, the guys always want a group picture—I’m always dodging it. I’ll pretend I need to grab a tool from the truck or hit the porta-john just so I don't end up in the shot. I can't stand the thought of that patch being immortalized on someone's Facebook page. 

And it's not just work, either. It bleeds into my home life, too. We usually do these family game nights on Fridays, me and the wife and the kids, maybe my brother comes over and we play cards. But lately, I’ve just been skipping them entirely. I'll hole up in the bedroom and say I'm too beat from hauling materials all day, but the truth is, sitting around a bright kitchen table with everyone right there, face-to-face... I just don't want people looking at my face. I can't sit there trying to play a game when all I can think about is whether they're staring at how caved-in and ruined my skin looks. It just eats at me, Doc. It really does.

Can you tell me if the concern you feel about this patch on your face is more about how it looks compared to the rest of your face, or if it's more about a fear that something might happen because of it, like it could get worse, or that people might judge you in a specific way?

Well, see, that's the thing, Doc... it's not really about being scared of what it's gonna turn into, you know? Like, I'm not sitting there thinking, "Oh man, is this some kind of cancer?" or "Is my whole face gonna fall off?" I mean, I've had guys on the crew get melanomas and stuff, and they have to go get pieces cut out, and that's scary, sure, but that's not what's going through my head when I'm looking at this. 

It's really just... it's just the way it looks right now. Just the sheer ugliness of it compared to the rest of me. I mean, my face isn't exactly a movie star's face to begin with, right? I've got wrinkles, I've got sunspots, I've got a scar on my chin from when a piece of rebar caught me back in '98... but all of that looks normal. It looks like a guy who's worked hard his whole life. But this patch... it just looks so wrong. It looks caved in and rough, and it just doesn't match anything else. 

And as for people judging me... I don't know if I'd call it a specific fear of them thinking I'm a bad guy or something. It's more just... I know they can see it. How could they not? It's right there. And when I'm at the grocery store, or picking up lumber at the supply yard, and the guy behind the counter looks at me, I just know his eyes are darting right to that spot. I can feel it. I know he's thinking, "Man, what happened to that guy's face?" And even if he doesn't say it out loud—which they usually don't, people are usually polite enough to keep their mouths shut—I just know that's all they're seeing. It's just the sheer embarrassment of walking around looking like this, having this glaring, ruined spot right in the middle of everything else. It just feels like it defines my whole face now, you know what I mean?

When you look at that patch on your face and see it as ruined or caved in, have others ever pointed out that it doesn't look that way to them, or have they ever seemed surprised by how much you focus on it?

Yeah, exactly, like I was saying when I first sat down, that's honestly one of the most frustrating parts of this whole ordeal. It happens all the time. Just last weekend, for example, my wife Mary and I were getting ready to run some errands, and I was stuck in the bathroom again. I had my face right up close to the glass, pointing right at the mirror, trying to show her exactly what I mean. I was tracing the edge of it, showing her how rough and sunken-looking that whole patch is, trying to get her to see how it makes that entire side of my face look completely old and beat-up. And she just sighed, crossed her arms, and looked at me like I was speaking Greek. She told me she barely notices anything at all, maybe a little shadow or some dry skin if she really squints, and that I need to stop obsessing over it. 

And it’s the exact same thing with the guys on the crew. If I ever accidentally end up in a photo—which I try my hardest to avoid, like I said, because I just can't stop seeing it whenever I look at a picture of myself—but if I do, and I point the patch out to them, they act totally shocked. They’re like, "What are you even talking about, man? It’s just your face." 

It drives me absolutely up the wall, Doc. Because I’m not blind, you know? I look in the mirror, or I look at those photos on someone's phone, and it is glaringly obvious to me. It's literally the only thing I can see. But my family, my buddies, they all just keep brushing it off, saying they don't see it, or acting totally surprised that I'm still focused on it. It makes you feel crazy, honestly, when you can see something so clearly on your own face, and everyone around you is acting like it doesn't even exist or that you're making a big deal out of nothing. It's like we're looking at two completely different people.
Have you noticed yourself becoming overly concerned about anything else besides that patch on your face—like other parts of your body, your health in general, or things happening in your life?

Well, no, not really. I mean, honestly, Doc, it's just this one thing. You'd think at my age—being 52 and working construction my whole life—I'd be worrying about a million other things, right? Like, sure, my body's got some miles on it. My left knee has been giving me grief since... I don't know, maybe 2015? We were doing this big commercial framing job, and I came down a bit too hard off a ladder. So yeah, it clicks when I walk upstairs, and my lower back definitely aches if I'm hauling materials or pouring concrete all day, but... I don't sit around stressing over it. It's just part of the trade. I take a couple of ibuprofen with my morning coffee and I'm good to go. I don't lose sleep over my joints or anything like that.

And as for my general health, I mean, Mary made me go get a physical last year, and my blood pressure was fine, cholesterol was normal. I don't sit around thinking I'm gonna drop dead of a heart attack or anything like some guys my age do. And life stuff... the kids are doing okay, the bills get paid on time. We're not rich, obviously, but we get by just fine. I don't stress about the mortgage any more than the next guy. 

It really is just... it's just this patch. It's like my brain only has room to fixate on this one specific spot on my face. If I didn't have this rough, caved-in mess right here, I swear I'd be the most relaxed guy on the site. It's just so frustrating because everything else in my life, the rest of my body, it's all exactly what it should be for a guy who works for a living. It's just this one thing that's throwing everything off and ruining my mornings, you know? Like I was saying about being stuck in the bathroom mirror, if I could just get this one spot to look normal, I wouldn't have a care in the world.
